```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5, message = FALSE)
has_gg <- requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)
```

Forecasting causes of death one at a time gives cause-specific forecasts
that do not add up to the all-cause forecast. mortensor offers three ways
to coherent cause-specific forecasts:

* **bottom-up**: separate models per cause, with all causes as their sum
  (`reconciled(..., method = "bottom_up")`);
* **reconciliation**: separate models for every cause and for all causes,
  projected draw by draw so that they add up (`method = "wls"`, `"mint"`,
  ...);
* **cause shares**: all-cause mortality with any model, and the shares of
  the causes with a compositional tensor model (`cause_shares()`).

This vignette compares them on deaths by cause and deprivation in England,
2001-2019 (`ons_data`; Source: Office for National Statistics licensed
under the Open Government Licence v3.0).

```{r}
library(mortensor)
library(data.table)
```

## Cause groups

The workbook has 29 causes, defined by mutually exclusive ICD-10 codes.
Several are rare, so cells by sex, quintile, 5-year age group and year would
often hold a handful of deaths. `ons_cause_groups` keeps the common cancers
and causes separate and combines small causes within their ICD-10 chapter.
The analysis starts at age 50, where the groups have enough deaths in almost
every cell (dementia and diabetes are sparse below 50).

The deaths of `ons_data` are in wide format, one column per cause.
`mt_data()` reads them by listing the cause columns as the levels of the
stratum variable `cause` (the all-cause column is named `"all"`); the
populations have no cause and are shared by all causes. `mt_subset()` keeps
ages 50 and over, and `mt_group_levels()` combines the causes. With
`total = "all"` and `other = "rest"`, the rest is all causes minus the
groups, so it also holds deaths from causes the table does not list
(including suicide).

```{r}
str(ons_cause_groups)
causes <- names(ons_data)[-(1:7)]
xc <- mt_data(deaths = ons_data, population = ons_data, by = c("sex", "imd_decile", "cause"),
              age = "age_group", value = list(deaths = c(all = "all_causes", causes), population = "population"))
xc <- mt_as_exposure(xc, type = "midyear")
xc <- mt_subset(xc, ages = c(50, Inf))
xc <- mt_group_levels(xc, "imd_decile", function(d) paste0("Q", ceiling(as.numeric(d) / 2)), name = "quintile")
xc <- mt_group_levels(xc, "cause", ons_cause_groups, other = "rest", total = "all", additive = "rates")
xc
```

Breast and prostate cancer form one group, the sex-specific cancer of each
sex (for men it also contains the few male breast cancers), so that both
sexes have the same causes.

Causes share the exposure of their stratum, so their **rates** add up to
the all-cause rate. The hierarchy says so with `additive = "rates"`, and
`mt_validate()` checks the sums:

```{r}
h <- mt_hierarchy(cause = "all", additive = "rates")
mt_validate(xc, hierarchy = h)
```

## Inequality by cause

Age-standardised death rates at ages 50 and over (European Standard
Population 2013) per cause and quintile, and the ratio between the most and
the least deprived quintile, 2017-2019:

```{r}
obs <- asr(mt_subset(xc, periods = c(2017, 2019)))[, .(asr = mean(q0.5)), by = .(sex, quintile, cause)]
ratio <- dcast(obs[quintile %in% c("Q1", "Q5")], sex + cause ~ quintile, value.var = "asr")
ratio[, `Q1 / Q5` := round(Q1 / Q5, 2)]
ratio[, c("Q1", "Q5") := lapply(.SD, round), .SDcols = c("Q1", "Q5")]
ratio[order(sex, -`Q1 / Q5`)]
```

The gradient is steepest for chronic lower respiratory disease, lung
cancer, liver disease and alcohol, and diabetes, and flattest for the
sex-specific cancers and colorectal cancer.

## Three approaches in a backtest

Forecasts from the origins 2008, 2011 and 2014 are scored on the following
five years, separately for the causes and for all causes:

```{r}
specs <- list(
  reconciled(lee_carter(), h, method = "bottom_up"),
  reconciled(lee_carter(), h, method = "wls"),
  reconciled(li_lee(common_by = c("sex", "cause")), h, method = "bottom_up"),
  cause_shares(total = li_lee(common_by = "sex"), ranks = c(5, 4, 6, 8)),
  lee_carter())
bt <- rbindlist(lapply(specs, function(sp) {
  b <- mt_backtest(sp, xc, origins = c(2008, 2011, 2014), h = 5, n_draws = 200)
  b[, level := ifelse(cause == "all", "all causes", "causes")]
}))
sc <- bt[, .(crps = round(mean(crps), 4), cov50 = round(mean(cov50), 2), cov95 = round(mean(cov95), 2)),
         by = .(model, level)]
dcast(sc, model ~ level, value.var = c("crps", "cov95"))
```

The last row, separate Lee-Carter models without reconciliation, is not
coherent: its all-cause forecasts come from a model of their own. On these
data the bottom-up sum of separate Lee-Carter models is coherent and
forecasts all causes more accurately than a model of all-cause mortality
itself: the trends of the causes differ (ischaemic heart disease fell much
faster than the rest), and their sum follows the changing composition.
Li-Lee with one common trend per sex and cause, also summed bottom-up, is
slightly more accurate for the single causes and less accurate for all
causes. The cause-share model is clearly less accurate here: it describes
the composition through a few factors shared by ages, years, groups and
causes, which these data, with large counts and diverse cause trends, do
not need. The 95% intervals of all approaches are too narrow for all causes
(see "Frequently asked questions" on interval calibration).

## Forecasts

Forecasts to 2034 with the bottom-up approach:

```{r}
fit <- mt_fit(reconciled(lee_carter(), h, method = "bottom_up"), xc)
fc <- mt_forecast(fit, h = 15, n_draws = 500, seed = 1)
fc$reconciliation
```

```{r, eval = has_gg, fig.height = 6}
mt_plot_shares(fc, groups = c("female.Q1", "female.Q5", "male.Q1", "male.Q5"),
               causes = c("ihd", "dementia", "lung_cancer", "respiratory", "rest"))
```

Dementia deaths rose steeply between 2001 and 2019. Separate models per
stratum extrapolate that rise for 15 years, which makes dementia the
largest group by 2034 with very wide intervals. Whether such a trend
continues is a substantive question (recorded trends of single causes can
reflect changes in diagnosis, certification and coding as well as in risk),
and the forecast should be read as a conditional statement.

Age-standardised rates and the ratio Q1 / Q5, path by path, so that the
intervals of the ratio include the joint uncertainty of both quintiles:

```{r}
rr <- mt_contrast(fc, var = "quintile", ref = "Q5", quantity = "asr", type = "ratio")[level == "Q1" & period == 2034]
rr <- rr[, .(sex, cause, q0.025 = round(q0.025, 2), q0.5 = round(q0.5, 2), q0.975 = round(q0.975, 2))]
merge(rr, ratio[, .(sex, cause, `2017-2019` = `Q1 / Q5`)], by = c("sex", "cause"))[order(sex, -q0.5)]
```

Separate models per stratum extrapolate each quintile's own trend, so the
ratios continue the recent changes of the gradient, with wide intervals.
Li-Lee with a common trend per sex and cause lets the quintiles deviate
from that trend only through stationary processes, which keeps the ratios
close to their average over the training years:

```{r}
fc_ll <- mt_forecast(mt_fit(specs[[3]], xc), h = 15, n_draws = 500, seed = 1)
rr_ll <- mt_contrast(fc_ll, var = "quintile", ref = "Q5", quantity = "asr", type = "ratio")[level == "Q1" &
                                                                                              period == 2034]
merge(rr[, .(sex, cause, lee_carter = q0.5)], rr_ll[, .(sex, cause, li_lee = round(q0.5, 2))],
      by = c("sex", "cause"))[order(sex, -lee_carter)]
```

Which assumption is more plausible is a judgement the backtest cannot
settle over five years. Deprivation deciles are also reclassified with each
new IMD version (2007, 2010, 2015 and 2019 in these data), and cause coding
changes over time, so trends of single causes in single quintiles deserve a
critical look before they are extrapolated.
